This walks through the pipeline from a standing start: what to install, what your
data has to look like, what to change, and what each part produces. Code here is
for copying — none of it executes when the site builds.

## 1. What you need

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
R 4.2 or later, and RStudio if you want the point-and-click render button. A full
run takes a few hours the first time, mostly BART sampling; afterwards caching
makes re-runs take seconds.
:::

```r
## CRAN packages
install.packages(c("BART", "dbarts", "bartMan", "caret", "rpart", "rpart.plot",
                   "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "purrr", "ggh4x", "gridExtra",
                   "scales", "bcf", "xgboost", "grf", "extraDistr", "devtools"))

## RIQITE is not on CRAN — it is the randomization-inference engine used in Part IV
devtools::install_github("li-xinran/RIQITE")
```

### The two source files

Both sit next to the `.Rmd` and are loaded by it. Download them directly:

```r
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harhay-lab/Covid-Steroid-HTE/main/clusterfunctions.R",
  destfile = "clusterfunctions.R")

download.file(
  paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Zhe-Chen-1999/",
         "Enhanced_inference_for_ITE_quantiles/main/helper_functions.R"),
  destfile = "helper_functions.R")
```

| File | What it provides |
|---|---|
| [`clusterfunctions.R`](https://github.com/harhay-lab/Covid-Steroid-HTE/blob/main/clusterfunctions.R) | `lbart.cluster()` and `wbart.cluster()` — run several BART chains in parallel and collect them into one posterior |
| [`helper_functions.R`](https://github.com/Zhe-Chen-1999/Enhanced_inference_for_ITE_quantiles/blob/main/helper_functions.R) | `method_combine()` and the rest of the ITE-quantile machinery |

## 2. What your data has to look like

One row per randomized patient, with no missing values in the analysis variables:

| Object | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `y` | numeric | the outcome — `0/1` for binary, any numeric for continuous |
| `z` | logical | treatment assignment, `TRUE` = treated |
| `X` | data.frame | baseline covariates |

Parts of the pipeline convert these internally: `z_num <- as.numeric(z)` is
created for Bayesian Causal Forest, causal forest, and the propensity models,
which require a numeric `0/1` indicator, and `model.matrix()` expands `X` into a
numeric design matrix for XGBoost and BCF. You supply the logical `z` and the
data-frame `X`; the conversions happen where they are needed.

## 3. The one block you edit

Everything downstream is driven by a single configuration chunk near the top:

```r
## ============================ EDIT THIS BLOCK =============================
## ---- Outcome type ----
OUTCOME_TYPE <- "binary"       # "binary" or "continuous"

## ---- Execution & Caching Parameters ----
GLOBAL_SEED <- 123
CACHE_DIR   <- "cache"   # expensive results are cached here
REFRESH_ALL <- FALSE     # TRUE recomputes every cached result on this knit

## ---- Which Parts to run ----
RUN_PRIOR_GRID    <- TRUE   # Part II: BART prior-sensitivity grid
RUN_CROSS_METHOD  <- TRUE   # Part II: Cross-method comparison (BCF, Causal Forest, XGBoost)
RUN_BASELINE_RISK <- TRUE   # Part III: Baseline-risk heterogeneity analysis
## =========================================================================
```

What each one does:

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| `OUTCOME_TYPE` | Governs Parts I–III: the BART likelihood (logit vs. Gaussian), the XGBoost objective, the prognostic-score family, and the summary tables. Risk-ratio output appears only for a binary outcome |
| `GLOBAL_SEED` | Seeds the BART chains, the cross-validation folds, and the unit shuffle in Part IV. Report it with any result |
| `CACHE_DIR` | Where cached results are written |
| `REFRESH_ALL` | `TRUE` recomputes everything on this knit, ignoring the cache |
| `RUN_PRIOR_GRID` | `FALSE` skips §2.1, the eight-configuration BART prior grid — the single most expensive block |
| `RUN_CROSS_METHOD` | `FALSE` skips §2.2, the BCF / causal forest / XGBoost comparison |
| `RUN_BASELINE_RISK` | `FALSE` skips all of Part III |

Setting the three `RUN_*` flags to `FALSE` reduces a knit to Parts I and IV,
which is useful while drafting text.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
`ALPHA` (the confidence level) and `NPERM` (the number of permutation draws) are
**not** in this block — they sit in Part IV's own setup chunk, since nothing
before Part IV uses them.
:::

### How the cache works

A full run takes hours, almost all of it BART sampling. Nobody will iterate on
prose if every re-knit costs an afternoon, so each expensive result is wrapped in
a small helper:

```r
step1.res <- cached("step1_bart_binary", {
  bart_fit_binary_outcome(X, y, z, ...)     # only runs if the file is absent
})
```

The first time through, the block runs and the result is written to
`cache/step1_bart_binary.rds`. Every later knit finds that file and reloads it in
milliseconds. The appendix prints a table of what was computed and what was
reloaded on that run.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
### The one thing to watch

**The cache is keyed on the name, not on the inputs.** It has no idea what went
into producing the result. Change your data, a seed, or a hyperparameter and the
*old* result is silently reloaded — no error, no warning, just stale numbers under
a new label.

So after any such change, set `REFRESH_ALL <- TRUE`, knit once, then set it back.
:::

To recompute one result rather than all of them, either pass `refresh = TRUE` to
that call:

```r
step1.res <- cached("step1_bart_binary", { ... }, refresh = TRUE)
```

or delete its file, which has the same effect:

```bash
rm cache/step1_bart_binary.rds
```

And if you change an analysis in a way that makes the old result meaningless — a
different estimator, a different analysis set — give it a **new name** rather than
reusing the old one, so the stale file cannot be loaded by accident.

## 4. Part I — a "fit-the-fit" approach

**§1.1** fits BART to the outcome and returns a posterior conditional average
treatment effect for every patient:

```r
step1.res <- bart_fit_binary_outcome(
  X, y, z,
  Power  = 3, Base = 0.25, Ntrees = 50,   # selected by 10-fold cross-validation
  seed = GLOBAL_SEED, nchains = 4,
  ndpost = 1000, nskip = 500
)
cate.res <- step1.res$cate_results
```

Passing vectors rather than scalars for `Power`/`Base`/`Ntrees` triggers the
cross-validation search, which takes over two hours.

This section also carries the **MCMC diagnostics** — autocorrelation of the
fitted response surface and Geweke statistics per chain. They belong here because
they check the sampler behind the estimates in this same section, before anything
is built on top of them. Slow autocorrelation decay means raising the thinning
interval.

**§1.2** fits a regression tree to those estimates, which is where the
interpretable subgroups come from:

```r
cart_fit(point_est = cate.res$cate,
         posterior = step1.res$cate_posterior,
         X = X_unscaled, metric = EFFECT_LABEL,
         maxdepth = 3, cp = 0.01)
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
The tree's splits are **hypotheses about effect modification**, not tested
subgroup effects. There is no multiplicity control here, and a single CART is
unstable — perturb the data slightly and a split can flip.
:::

**§1.3** produces VIVI–VSUP heatmaps: the diagonal is a posterior split-inclusion
proportion for each covariate, and the off-diagonal is pairwise interaction
strength — something a variable-importance barplot cannot show. Colour intensity
encodes magnitude and desaturation encodes posterior uncertainty.

## 5. Part II — sensitivity analyses and cross-method comparison

Two checks on whether the Part I picture survives scrutiny.

**§2.1 — the BART prior.** Eight prior configurations, varying tree depth
(`power`, `base`), leaf shrinkage (`k`), and ensemble size (`ntree`). The
shrinkage ratio — the spread of posterior-mean CATEs across patients divided by
the average within-patient posterior SD — summarises each. If it stays near zero
across the whole grid, the posterior cannot separate patients and any apparent
subgroup structure is fragile.

**§2.2 — other estimators.** Bayesian Causal Forest, XGBoost T- and S-learners,
and causal forest are fitted to the same data, and their CATE distributions are
overlaid. Agreement is reassuring; disagreement localises which modelling choice
is driving the result.

## 6. Part III — treatment effect heterogeneity by prognostic score

Effect heterogeneity often tracks a patient's overall prognosis rather than any
individual covariate.

**§3.1** estimates a prognostic score three ways — from the control arm only,
from the full sample without a treatment indicator, and from a sample split that
reserves part of the control arm for fitting. Comparing the three guards against
the score being an artifact of how it was estimated.

**§3.2** groups patients into quartiles of that score and reports the observed
treatment effect within each, with bootstrap confidence intervals.

**§3.3** estimates the CATE as a smooth function of the score, and fits a CART to
discover subgroups defined by baseline prognosis.

## 7. Part IV — randomization-based inference for ITE quantiles

The part with no outcome model. It uses only the trial's randomization.

```r
## Shuffle first: the rank statistic breaks ties by index order
set.seed(GLOBAL_SEED)
ord <- sample(length(z))
Z <- as.numeric(z)[ord]; Y <- as.numeric(y_cont)[ord]; n <- length(Z)

## One-sided lower confidence limits for every effect quantile
ci_lower <- method_combine(
  Z = Z, Y = Y, N = n, k_vec = 1:n,
  alpha = ALPHA, simul = TRUE, nperm = NPERM,
  treat.method.list   = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6),
  control.method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6)
)

plot_quantile_bound(ci_lower$lower, bound_type = "lower")
```

Upper limits come from re-running with the treatment labels switched, then
negating and reversing:

```r
ub <- method_combine(Z = 1 - Z, Y = Y, N = n, k_vec = 1:n,
                     alpha = ALPHA, simul = TRUE, nperm = NPERM,
                     treat.method.list   = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6),
                     control.method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6))
upper <- -ub$lower[n:1]
```

Two-sided intervals combine a lower and an upper limit, each at `ALPHA/2`, by
Bonferroni.

### Turning limits into a count

If the lower limit satisfies $L_k > c$ then $\tau_{(k)} > c$, and because the
effects are sorted, so does every larger one — hence *at least* $n - k + 1$
patients have an effect above $c$:

```r
n_benefit <- sapply(thresholds, function(cc) {
  kk <- which(ci_lower$lower > cc)
  if (length(kk)) n - min(kk) + 1L else 0L
})
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
### Read the direction from the right limit

If a **larger outcome is good**, benefit is $\tau_i > c$ — read it from the
**lower** limits. If a **larger outcome is bad**, benefit is $\tau_i < c$ — read
it from the **upper** limits.

Spend the whole of $\alpha$ on the direction of interest. Reading one side off a
two-sided interval uses $\alpha/2$ and is needlessly conservative.
:::

A second worked example applies the same machinery to the distracted-driving
trial, whose outcome is continuous and effectively free of ties — the setting in
which the rank statistic is least affected by tie-breaking.
